title: The LORD Will Rejoice Over You with Singing
summary: Zephaniah pronounces woe on Jerusalem, the rebellious city whose officials, judges, prophets, and priests have betrayed their callings, even though the righteous LORD is within her every morning. God declares that he will gather the nations for judgment, and then promises to give the peoples pure lips to call on his name, to remove the proud, and to leave a meek and humble remnant. The book ends with a song calling Zion to rejoice, because the LORD her King is among her, mighty to save, and will rejoice over her with singing as he gathers the scattered and restores their fortunes.
story: Chapter 1 announced the Day of the LORD against Judah; chapter 2 called the humble to seek the LORD and turned judgment toward the nations. Chapter 3 returns to Jerusalem, and at first it sounds like the nations' oracles continued, since it begins with the same cry of woe. Jerusalem is no better than Nineveh. But in verse 9 the book turns decisively. The same fire that consumes the earth becomes a purifying fire, and the book ends in a burst of joy. This movement from judgment to restoration matches the pattern of the whole prophetic tradition, and it speaks to the generation that would live through Jerusalem's fall and the exile, promising that God's last word to them would be gathering, not scattering.
historical:
The corruption described in verses 1 to 7 fits Jerusalem in the seventh century BC, under the influence of Manasseh's long reign and before or during Josiah's reform (about 640 to 609 BC). Every level of leadership is named: princes (royal officials), judges, prophets, and priests. Jeremiah, a younger contemporary, makes similar charges against the same classes (Jeremiah 5:31, 23:11). Verse 6's reference to nations already cut off reminds Jerusalem of what it had seen: Samaria's fall in 722 BC and Assyria's destruction of many cities in the region.

The promises of verses 9 to 20 look beyond the coming disaster. Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC, and many of its people were scattered in exile. The promise to gather the scattered and restore their fortunes spoke to that situation, and some scholars think this final section was expanded for readers during or after the exile. Others see no reason why Zephaniah himself could not have looked beyond the judgment he announced, as earlier prophets like Isaiah and Micah had. Either way, the return from exile after 539 BC was read as the beginning of these promises, though their full scope reaches further.
cultural:
The images of Jerusalem's leaders draw on the fears of a herding society. Roaring lions and evening wolves, which hunt at dusk and leave nothing by morning, describe officials and judges who devour the vulnerable instead of protecting them. Prophets were expected to speak God's word faithfully, and priests to guard the holiness of the sanctuary and teach the law (Malachi 2:7); Zephaniah charges them with recklessness and with doing violence to the law. By contrast, the LORD within her dispenses justice morning by morning, like a faithful judge who holds court at the city gate each day.

The promise of pure lips in verse 9 uses the same Hebrew word for lip (safah) that Genesis 11 uses for language at Babel, where one lip was confused and scattered. Zephaniah reverses Babel: God gives the peoples purified speech so that they can call on his name together. Cush, south of Egypt, represented the far edge of the known world, so worshipers from beyond the rivers of Cush means worshipers from the ends of the earth. The appointed feasts (verse 18) were the great pilgrim festivals that exile made impossible. The Daughter of Zion is a poetic personification of Jerusalem and its people, a common image in the prophets.
literary: The chapter has three sections. Verses 1 to 8 are a woe oracle against Jerusalem, contrasting the unfaithfulness of the city's leaders with the faithfulness of the LORD in her midst, and ending with God's decision to gather the nations for judgment. Verses 9 to 13 describe the purification of the peoples and the remnant, using the phrase on that day and repeated images of humility, trust, and truthful speech. Verses 14 to 20 are a song of joy in the style of the Psalms, with a call to sing (verse 14), a reason (verses 15 to 17), and God's own promises (verses 18 to 20). The phrase among you or within her (from the word qerev) appears repeatedly: the LORD is within the corrupt city (verse 5), the proud are removed from among her (verse 11), the humble are left within her (verse 12), and the LORD is among her as King and Savior (verses 15 and 17). The whole book turns on what it means for God to be in the midst of his people.

outline.t: Woe to the rebellious city and its faithless leaders
Jerusalem refused correction; wait for the day of judgment
Pure lips for the peoples; worshipers from beyond Cush
The proud removed, a meek and humble remnant left
Sing, O Daughter of Zion: the LORD rejoices over you
God gathers the scattered and restores their fortunes

doctrines.note: The book that began with universal judgment ends with a song of joy. Hope rests not on Jerusalem's reform but on God's promise to purify, gather, and dwell among his people.
The LORD is mighty to save (verse 17). He takes away punishment, turns back enemies, saves the lame, and gathers the scattered. Salvation is God's own work, flowing from his presence and love.
God promises pure lips to the peoples so that all may call on his name and serve him together. Salvation reaches from Israel to the nations, reversing the division of Babel.
Verse 17 is one of the Bible's most striking pictures of God: not only a judge but one who rejoices over his people with gladness and singing, and quiets them with his love.

words.note: Qerev, inward part, midst, among. It appears six times in this chapter and carries the book's central theme. The LORD is righteous within the city even while its leaders are corrupt (verse 5), and in the restoration he is Israel's King among you (verse 15) and The LORD your God is among you (verse 17). God's presence is both the reason for judgment and the source of joy.

Safah, lip, speech, language. The word for language in the Babel story (Genesis 11:1, 7, 9) appears here in the promise to restore pure lips to the peoples. Where Babel's confused speech scattered humanity, God's purified speech gathers them to call on his name.

Charash, to be quiet or silent. In verse 17 the BSB reads He will quiet you with His love. The Hebrew literally says he will be quiet in his love, and interpreters differ: some understand God quieting his people's fears, others God resting silently in his love for them, others (following the Greek translation) God renewing them. All readings picture God's love as settled and at peace.

Ani, afflicted, poor, or lowly, rendered meek in verse 12, where it stands beside dal, poor or weak. The word describes people who are low in status and dependent, and in the Psalms and prophets it often names those who have no one but God to rely on. Zephaniah's remnant is marked by lowliness and trust rather than power, the opposite of those who rejoice in their pride (verse 11).

christ: The call to the Daughter of Zion to sing because her King is among her finds a close parallel in Zechariah 9:9, which tells the Daughter of Zion to rejoice because her king is coming, humble and riding on a donkey. The Gospels apply Zechariah's words to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:5, John 12:15), and many readers hear Zephaniah's song in the background. John's Gospel says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), a fulfillment of the hope that God himself would be in the midst of his people. The promise of purified lips so that the peoples may call on the name of the LORD is often linked with Pentecost, when the Spirit enabled the apostles to speak in many languages and people from many nations heard the gospel (Acts 2), a reversal of Babel in the same spirit as Zephaniah 3:9. Revelation 14:5 says of the redeemed that no lie was found in their mouths, close to verse 13's description of the remnant. And the God who rejoices over his people with singing is the God of Jesus' parables in Luke 15, where heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. These links are thematic rather than direct quotations, but they show how deeply this chapter's hope runs into the New Testament.

hard.q: How can the same book announce the destruction of all the earth and then promise joy and gathering?
hard.a: Some readers find the shift from Zephaniah 1 to Zephaniah 3 so abrupt that they conclude the hopeful ending was added later by a different hand, and many critical scholars hold that view for at least part of verses 14 to 20. Others argue that the move from judgment to restoration is typical of the prophets (compare Amos 9, Hosea 14, Micah 7) and fits Zephaniah's own logic. The key is verse 8 and verse 9: the fire of God's jealousy consumes the earth, and then God purifies the lips of the peoples. Judgment in the prophets is often purifying rather than simply destructive, like a refiner's fire that removes dross. The remnant that remains is the humble who sought the LORD in chapter 2. On either view of the book's composition, the final form teaches that God's judgment and his joy are not opposed; judgment clears the way for a people in whom he can delight.

questions: Jerusalem's leaders failed even though the LORD was righteous within the city. What does it mean for a community to have God among it and still resist him?
Zephaniah 3:17 says the LORD will rejoice over you with singing. How does it change your picture of God to imagine him rejoicing over his people?
The remnant is described as meek, humble, trusting, and truthful. Which of these marks do you most want to grow in, and why?
